glance.label: Main Idea
glance.html: Proverbs 31 ends the book with wisdom on a throne and in a household: a mother teaches King Lemuel that his strength and clear mind belong to the defenseless, and an alphabet poem praises a woman of valor who fears the LORD.

glance.label: Setting
glance.html: Lemuel is otherwise unknown, and the text does not identify him with Solomon. The closing poem, which may or may not continue his mother’s words, follows her counsel to the king (31:1–9) and stands in contrast to the adulterous woman of the previous chapter (30:20).

glance.html: “Charm is deceitful and beauty is passing, But a woman who fears the LORD, she shall be praised.” (Proverbs 31:30)

cards.title: The Heart of the Chapter
cards.html:
Proverbs began with a father and mother teaching a son (1:8), and it ends with a mother’s voice. Lemuel’s mother cries, “What, my son? And what, son of my womb? And what, son of my vows?” (31:2), and her love speaks as hard counsel. A king’s strength and clear mind are not his to waste, because wine can make him “forget the law” (31:5), and his mouth is to be opened “for the speechless” (31:8).

Then, after the mother’s counsel to her son, comes the woman of valor, a contrast with the adulterous woman of the previous chapter who wipes her mouth and denies any wrong (30:20). Her alphabet poem gives a complete picture of wisdom lived: strong, trusted, skilled in trade, generous to the poor, and kind in speech. She is a real woman first, praised by a husband who knows her (31:29). At a deeper, layered level, she is the bride worth finding. “Who can find a virtuous wife?” (31:10) recalls Wisdom’s promise, “whoever finds me finds life” (8:35), and she pictures the Church that Christ presents to Himself as “a glorious church” (Ephesians 5:27).

The poem’s last word explains all the rest: “a woman who fears the LORD, she shall be praised” (31:30). The book that called the fear of the LORD the beginning of knowledge (1:7) closes with a life built on that right view of God.

cards.title: Chapter Sections
cards.html:
Proverbs 31:1–7 — A Mother’s Counsel to a King

Lemuel’s mother, who calls him “son of my vows” (31:2), warns him not to spend his strength on women or his judgment on wine, because a king who drinks forgets the law and the afflicted pay the price. Strong drink belongs instead to the dying and the bitter of heart, most likely as relief in their suffering, and the verses give no general approval of drinking away trouble.

Proverbs 31:8–9 — Open Your Mouth for the Speechless

Her warnings give way to a charge: the mouth a king keeps clear of wine is to be opened for people who have no voice, even “all who are appointed to die” (31:8). In her teaching, a ruler’s authority is held for the sake of the poor and needy who cannot defend themselves.

Proverbs 31:10–12 — Who Can Find a Virtuous Wife?

The poem opens by asking where such a woman can be found and answers with her worth, far above rubies, and with a husband whose trust in her is never disappointed, because she does him good all her days. Read at a deeper, layered level, she pictures the Church, precious because Christ purchased her “with His own blood” (Acts 20:28).

Proverbs 31:13–27 — Her Strength, Diligence, and Kindness

Fifteen verses show her at work: spinning wool and flax, rising before daylight to feed her household, buying a field and planting a vineyard, selling linen garments, opening her hands to the needy, and speaking with “the law of kindness” on her tongue (31:26). The layered reading sees the watchful Bride ready for the Bridegroom in her lamp that “does not go out by night” (31:18; Matthew 25:6), a household covered by the blood of Christ in the scarlet of 31:21, the Bride’s fine linen (Revelation 19:7–8) in her clothing (31:22), and Christ seated at the Father’s right hand in the husband who “is known in the gates” (31:23).

Proverbs 31:28–31 — A Woman Who Fears the LORD Shall Be Praised

Her children and her husband praise her first, and he tells her that many daughters have done well but she excels them all. The last verses name the ground of that praise, the fear of the LORD rather than charm or beauty, and send her own works to praise her in the gates, the public place where Wisdom first cried out (1:21).

cards.title: Why This Chapter Matters
cards.html:
Proverbs 31 shows what strength and plenty are for. Lemuel’s mother teaches that authority is held for those who cannot speak for themselves, and the woman of valor turns the profit of her hands into food for her household and open hands for the poor (31:20). In this chapter wisdom always reaches past the self.

The chapter also guards how its poem is read. Her praise rests on the fear of the LORD, not on how much she accomplishes, so her portrait is never a checklist to burden women, and the same honor belongs to every woman who fears Him, whether single, widowed, or married (31:30). Because she also pictures the Bride, her burning lamp and her household clothed in scarlet describe a Church that keeps watch for her Bridegroom, covered by His blood.

cards.title: Key Themes to Watch For
cards.html:
Strength rightly used. Lemuel must not give his strength to women, while the woman of valor girds herself with strength and wears strength and honor as clothing (31:3, 17, 25).

Opened mouths. The king opens his mouth for the speechless and the poor, and the woman opens hers with wisdom and kindness (31:8–9, 26).

Willing hands. Her hands work wool and flax and hold the spindle, and the same hands reach out to the needy, until the fruit of her hands is given back to her as praise (31:13, 19–20, 31).

Honor in the gates. Her husband is known among the elders in the gates, and in the end her own works praise her there (31:23, 31).

The fear of the LORD. Charm and beauty pass, but the woman who fears the LORD is praised, and the book closes on the truth with which it opened (31:30; 1:7).

cards.title: Key Words & Concepts
cards.html:
King Lemuel (31:1). A king known only from this chapter and not identified in the text with Solomon. His words are an “utterance” (31:1) his mother taught him.

Son of my vows (31:2). The third of the mother’s tender addresses, describing a son she carried and prayed for with vows. Her warnings come from that love.

Virtuous wife (31:10). The Hebrew word behind “virtuous” (chayil) means strength, valor, and worth, which is why she is often called the woman of valor. The same word returns in “Many daughters have done well” (31:29) and describes Ruth as “a virtuous woman” (Ruth 3:11).

The alphabet poem (31:10–31). In Hebrew the twenty-two verses form an acrostic, each beginning with the next letter of the alphabet. The form presents her portrait as complete, from the first letter to the last.

Scarlet (31:21). Rich, warm cloth that lets her face winter without fear for her household. At the layered level, the scarlet pictures her household covered by the blood of Christ.

The fear of the LORD (31:30). A right view of God: terror for those who defy Him and awe for all at His glory, majesty, and holiness, for He is unlike any other. It is the beginning of knowledge (1:7) and the true source of this woman’s worth.

sections.title: A Mother’s Counsel to a King
Open Your Mouth for the Speechless
Who Can Find a Virtuous Wife?
A Woman Who Fears the LORD Shall Be Praised

1.brief: The book’s last collection is the teaching of King Lemuel, the utterance his mother taught him. Lemuel is otherwise unknown, and here a queen mother’s wisdom trains a king, just as a mother’s teaching was honored at the book’s beginning (1:8).
1.explain:
“The words of King Lemuel,”

The book’s final collection carries the name of King Lemuel. He is otherwise unknown; Scripture names him only in this chapter, and the text does not identify him with Solomon or any other known king of Israel or Judah. What matters is that a king is being taught, and the teaching is meant to govern how he uses his power.

“the utterance which his mother taught him:”

The words are called an “utterance,” a weighty and solemn saying, and they come from his mother. Proverbs opened with a father’s instruction and the charge, “do not forsake the law of your mother” (1:8). Now, at the end of the book, a mother’s voice is heard directly. A queen mother, who held real influence in ancient royal courts, trains her son for the throne. Lemuel passes on what she taught him, honoring her by preserving her words. Wisdom handed from parent to child, which has run through the whole book, reaches its last example here.
1.notes: The Hebrew word translated “utterance” is the same word used in Agur’s heading (30:1), often translated oracle or burden, a weighty message. The ESV and NASB read “oracle,” and the KJV “prophecy.” Some read it as the name of a people or region, Massa (Genesis 25:14), which would make Lemuel a king of Massa.

2.brief: She opens with an urgent, tender cry: “What, my son? And what, son of my womb? And what, son of my vows?” The threefold address shows a mother pouring out her heart for the son she carried and prayed for with vows.
2.explain:
“What, my son? And what, son of my womb? And what, son of my vows?”

Lemuel’s mother opens with an urgent cry, repeating “what” three times as if she can hardly find the words. Her concern is sharp: what is her son doing, and what will he become? Each address draws closer to her heart. He is “my son,” her own child. He is “son of my womb,” the one she carried and bore. And he is “son of my vows,” a child she prayed for and dedicated to God with promises. Hannah offers a picture of such a mother, who “made a vow” (1 Samuel 1:11) and gave her son to the LORD. The warnings that follow are hard counsel, but they come from a mother’s love. She speaks plainly because she cares too much to stay silent.
2.notes: The ESV expands each question to ask what the son is doing, while the NLT renders the verse as a series of tender addresses beginning “O my son.”

3.brief: Her first warning is not to spend his strength on women or give his ways to what destroys kings. Indulgence drains a ruler’s strength and turns his heart, a danger Solomon’s own many wives displayed (1 Kings 11:1–4).
3.explain:
“Do not give your strength to women,”

Her first warning concerns how the king spends himself. His “strength” is his vigor, his time, his resources, and his attention. A king who gives himself to many women, whether a large harem or a life of sexual indulgence, drains the strength that belongs to his people and his calling. Israel’s law warned that a king must not “multiply wives for himself, lest his heart turn away” (Deuteronomy 17:17). The warning concerns indulgence and the misuse of power; it is not a slight against women, and the chapter will end by praising a woman of strength.

“Nor your ways to that which destroys kings.”

Indulgence does not stay private. It turns a ruler’s heart and ruins his reign. Solomon’s own history displayed the danger: “his wives turned away his heart” (1 Kings 11:3). The mother wants her son to keep his ways for the purposes God gave him, not hand them over to what has brought down kings before him.
3.notes: The ESV takes the danger as people rather than a thing, reading “those” who destroy kings.

4.brief: Wine and strong drink are not for kings and princes, she tells Lemuel by name. A ruler’s clear mind belongs to the people he has been given to serve.
4.explain:
“It is not for kings, O Lemuel,”

The mother calls her son by name, and the repetition “It is not for kings” gives the warning weight. What may be permitted to others is not fitting for a man who holds the power of judgment over a nation.

“It is not for kings to drink wine, Nor for princes intoxicating drink;”

Wine and strong drink cloud the mind and loosen restraint. Proverbs has already warned that “Wine is a mocker, Strong drink is a brawler” (20:1). For a ruler the danger is multiplied, because his decisions fall on others. Isaiah pronounced woe on “men mighty at drinking wine” who “justify the wicked for a bribe” (Isaiah 5:22–23). A king’s clear mind is not his own to spend; it belongs to the people he has been given to serve. The warning focuses on rulers and their duty, and the next verse states the reason.
4.notes: The ESV, NASB, and KJV read “strong drink” for “intoxicating drink,” and the NASB speaks of rulers who “desire” it.

5.brief: Drink could make a king forget the law and twist justice for all the afflicted. The cost of a clouded judgment falls on the weakest people in the land.
5.explain:
“Lest they drink and forget the law,”

Drink makes a king forget what he must never forget, the law he is charged to uphold. A ruler’s first duty is to remember what is right and to judge by it. Wine dulls the memory and the conscience at the very point where the people need them most.

“And pervert the justice of all the afflicted.”

The cost of a clouded mind falls on the weakest. The “afflicted” are the poor, the oppressed, and those without power to defend themselves, and their only hope is a judge who will see clearly and rule fairly. A drunken king perverts their justice, twisting their cases or neglecting them altogether. Every one of them is affected, for the verse speaks of “all the afflicted.” Lemuel’s mother is teaching that the purpose of royal sobriety is justice for those who cannot protect themselves.
5.notes: The Hebrew word behind “the law” means what has been decreed, and the ESV and NASB render it that way; they also read “rights” for “justice.” The KJV margin gives the literal Hebrew phrase behind “all the afflicted”: all the sons of affliction.

6.brief: Strong drink is to be given to the one who is perishing, and wine to those whose hearts are bitter. Over against the king who must stay clear-headed, she most likely points to the dying and the deeply afflicted, for whom drink could bring a measure of relief; it is no general prescription for drinking away poverty or distress.
6.explain:
“Give strong drink to him who is perishing,”

Over against the king who must stay clear-headed, his mother names those for whom drink may serve a different purpose. The one “who is perishing” is most likely someone dying or in the last stages of suffering. For such a person, strong drink could bring a measure of relief from pain. The contrast is with the ruler: the king must keep his mind clear for others, while the dying man has no more duties of judgment to perform.

“And wine to those who are bitter of heart.”

The parallel line widens the circle to those whose hearts are bitter, people crushed by grief or deep affliction. The verse is not a general prescription for drinking away poverty or distress, and it does not overturn the book’s many warnings against drunkenness (23:29–35). It most likely describes compassion toward the dying and the deeply afflicted, set against the ruler’s calling to sobriety. Some have read 31:6–7 as ironic, but the plain contrast with 31:4–5 is the more natural reading.
6.notes:
The KJV describes him as “ready” to perish. Behind “bitter of heart” is a Hebrew phrase meaning literally bitter of soul, which the KJV gives in its margin. The ESV and NLT read “those in bitter distress.”

The Babylonian Talmud (Sanhedrin 43a) cites this verse for a later Jewish custom: a man being led out to execution was given wine mixed with frankincense to dull his senses. That later practice does not settle the verse’s original setting. Mark records that Jesus was offered “wine mingled with myrrh to drink, but He did not take it” (Mark 15:23); the Gospel does not explain that drink by this custom.

7.brief: Let such a one drink and forget his poverty and remember his misery no more. The contrast with verses 4–5 is deliberate: the king must remember the law and do justice, while the dying sufferer may be allowed for a while to forget his pain.
7.explain:
“Let him drink and forget his poverty,”

The suffering man may drink and forget, for a while, what weighs on him. The word “forget” links this verse to 31:5. The king must not drink, because he would forget the law; the sufferer may drink, so that he can forget his misery. The contrast is deliberate, and it keeps the focus on the king’s responsibility.

“And remember his misery no more.”

For the man at the end of his strength, relief from remembering his misery is a mercy. The verse describes temporary relief, not a cure, and it gives no endorsement to escaping life’s troubles through drink. The deeper answer for the poor and afflicted comes in the next two verses, where the king himself is charged to speak for them and defend their cause. The ruler who keeps his mind clear can do for the poor what wine never can.
7.notes:
The NASB reads “trouble” for “misery.” The ESV and NLT render the verse in the plural, applying it to all the afflicted of 31:6.

Proverbs 31:8–9 — Open Your Mouth for the Speechless

8.brief: Lemuel is to open his mouth for those who cannot speak for themselves, taking up the cause of all who are appointed to die. Turning from warnings to a positive charge, his mother shows what royal power is for: speaking up for the defenseless.
8.explain:
“Open your mouth for the speechless,”

The mother turns from warnings to a positive charge. Royal power is for speaking. The speechless are those who cannot speak for themselves, whether because they are powerless, poor, ignored, or silenced. The king is to be their voice in the place of judgment. A ruler who keeps his mind clear (31:4–5) is able to use his mouth for the people who have no voice.

“In the cause of all who are appointed to die.”

The king is to take up the legal cause of those marked for destruction, people facing death through injustice, oppression, or abandonment. They have no one else to plead for them. The charge applies to everyone who holds influence over others, and it should not be assigned to a single modern cause. Wherever people are about to be crushed without anyone to speak for them, those with power and a voice are called to open their mouths.
8.notes: The ESV and NASB read “mute” for “speechless.” Behind “appointed to die” is a Hebrew phrase meaning literally the sons of destruction, which the KJV gives in its margin, while the ESV reads “destitute,” taking the phrase to mean those who are perishing through want.

9.brief: She repeats the charge: open your mouth, judge righteously, and plead the cause of the poor and needy. A king’s voice in judgment exists to defend the weak, and her counsel ends where the book has often pointed, at justice for the poor.
9.explain:
“Open your mouth, judge righteously,”

The mother repeats the charge, “Open your mouth,” and adds what kind of speech she means. The king must judge righteously, deciding cases by what is right and not by bribes, favoritism, or pressure. His voice carries the authority of judgment, and it must be used justly.

“And plead the cause of the poor and needy.”

To plead a cause is to argue a case as an advocate. The king is not only a neutral judge; he is to take the side of the poor and needy, making sure their rights are heard and protected. Lemuel’s mother ends where the book has often pointed: the measure of a ruler is justice for the weakest. “The king who judges the poor with truth, His throne will be established forever” (29:14). Her counsel closes the words of Lemuel with a call to use power for others.
9.notes:
The ESV and NASB read “defend” and “rights” for “plead the cause,” bringing out the legal setting of the charge.

Proverbs 31:10–12 — Who Can Find a Virtuous Wife?

10.brief: The closing poem, an acrostic whose verses follow the Hebrew alphabet, opens by asking who can find a virtuous wife, a woman of strength and worth whose value is far above rubies. She is first a real woman of wisdom, and at the deeper, layered level she pictures the Church, the Bride of Christ, precious because He purchased her with His own blood (Acts 20:28).
10.explain:
“Who can find a virtuous wife?”

The book’s closing poem begins with a question. A “virtuous wife” is a woman of strength, valor, and worth. The Hebrew word behind “virtuous” describes capability and character together, the same word Boaz used when he called Ruth “a virtuous woman” (Ruth 3:11). The question “Who can find” does not mean such women do not exist; it means they are rare and precious, worth searching for. The young man of the book’s opening chapters was urged to find Wisdom, for “whoever finds me finds life” (8:35), and was told that “He who finds a wife finds a good thing” (18:22). Now the book shows him the woman worth finding.

“For her worth is far above rubies.”

Her value exceeds the most costly jewels. Proverbs used the same comparison of wisdom itself: “She is more precious than rubies” (3:15). The woman of this poem is wisdom lived out in a real life. She is first a real woman, strong, trusted, and wise, and the poem praises her as such. It is not a checklist laid on every woman, and its praise, grounded in the fear of the LORD (31:30), belongs equally to single women and widows who fear Him.

At a deeper, layered level, the poem also portrays the Church as the Bride of Christ. Her worth far above rubies pictures the Church as precious to God, “the church of God which He purchased with His own blood” (Acts 20:28). Christ seeks and finds His Bride, and He presents her to Himself as “a glorious church” (Ephesians 5:27).
10.notes:
The poem of 31:10–31 is an acrostic: its twenty-two verses begin with the twenty-two letters of the Hebrew alphabet in order, from the first letter in 31:10 to the last in 31:31.

The Hebrew phrase translated “virtuous wife” also appears in 12:4, where the NKJV renders it “An excellent wife,” and in Ruth 3:11. The Hebrew word for “virtuous” can describe strength, ability, wealth, or valor. It is the same word as “strength” in 31:3, where the king is warned not to give his strength to women, and it returns in 31:29, “Many daughters have done well.”

The ESV and NASB read “An excellent wife,” and they read “jewels” for “rubies.”

Whether 31:10–31 continues the words of Lemuel’s mother or stands as a separate poem is debated. The text gives the poem no heading of its own.

11.brief: Her husband trusts her with his whole heart, and through her he lacks nothing of value. Her faithfulness frees him from worry about his household; in the layered reading, Christ entrusts His Bride with the gospel and the care of His household on earth.
11.explain:
“The heart of her husband safely trusts her;”

Her husband’s trust is complete. “Heart” means his inner self, and he rests on her with full confidence. He does not need to check up on her, worry about the household, or fear what she does when he is away. Her faithfulness frees him. Trust like this grows from a long record of reliability, which 31:12 goes on to describe.

“So he will have no lack of gain.”

Because of her, he lacks nothing of value. Her diligence, wisdom, and good management bring real increase to the household, and the following verses show how. The gain is material, but it is also the richness of a life shared with a trustworthy wife.

In the layered reading of the poem, the trusting husband pictures Christ entrusting His Bride with the gospel, the care of souls, and the management of His estate on earth, as this woman manages her husband’s house and fields (31:16).
11.notes: The Hebrew word translated “gain” usually means spoil or plunder taken in war, as the KJV’s “spoil” shows. The image fits a poem about a woman of strength and valor, though here the word describes the household’s gain rather than literal plunder.

12.brief: She does him good and never harm, every day of her life. Her goodness is steady and lifelong, which is why the trust of verse 11 is well placed.
12.explain:
“She does him good and not evil”

Her treatment of her husband is consistently good. The verse states it both positively and negatively: she brings him good, and she never brings him harm. She is not a source of trouble, shame, or strife in his life, unlike the contentious wife Proverbs warns about elsewhere. Her goodness is active, seeking his welfare in practical ways.

“All the days of her life.”

Her goodness is not seasonal or dependent on mood. It lasts every day of her life. This steady faithfulness, day after day and year after year, is why the trust of 31:11 is well placed. The poem praises a character proven over time, not a single act. In the book’s portrait of wisdom, lasting faithfulness is worth more than any display.
12.notes:
The ESV and NLT read “harm” for “evil,” making clear that the line concerns the effect of her conduct on her husband.

Proverbs 31:13–27 — Her Strength, Diligence, and Kindness

13.brief: Wool and flax are what she seeks out, and she works them with willing hands. Her industry is glad and freely given, and the layered reading sees in wool and linen the outward deeds of mercy and the inward purity of heart woven together in the Christian life.
13.explain:
“She seeks wool and flax,”

The poem now turns to her works. Wool from sheep and flax for linen were the raw materials for clothing in ancient Israel. She does not wait for them to arrive; she seeks them out, choosing good materials for the work ahead.

“And willingly works with her hands.”

Her work is glad and freely given. “Willingly” describes hands that work with delight, not under compulsion. Her industry flows from a willing heart. This is the opposite of the lazy man of the book’s earlier portraits, who craves but will not work.

As a layered reading, Augustine saw in the wool and the linen two sides of the Christian life woven together: wool, an outer garment, picturing outward deeds of mercy, and linen picturing inward purity of heart and faith. The Bride’s work joins what is seen and what is hidden into one garment.
13.notes: In Hebrew she works with the delight of her palms, that is, with hands that are glad to work. The ESV speaks of “willing hands,” and the NASB reads “in delight.”

14.brief: Like the merchant ships, she brings her food from far away. She looks beyond what is close at hand to supply her household with the best she can find.
14.explain:
“She is like the merchant ships,”

The comparison is to trading ships that sailed to distant ports and returned with goods from other lands. She has the same reach. She is not limited to what grows in her own field or what the local market offers.

“She brings her food from afar.”

Like those ships, she brings food from a distance, seeking out the best provisions for her household through trade and careful planning. Her vision extends beyond what is close at hand. The verse shows initiative and enterprise in the service of the people she cares for.

In the layered reading approved for this poem, the merchant ships picture the Church gathering spiritual nourishment from among the nations, bringing what feeds her household from afar.
14.notes: The NLT reads “a merchant’s ship,” and the ESV speaks of the ships of the merchant.

15.brief: Before daylight she rises to provide food for her household and portions for her maidservants. Her care begins before the day does and reaches everyone under her roof, including those who serve.
15.explain:
“She also rises while it is yet night,”

She rises before daylight. In a household that baked its own bread and prepared every meal from raw materials, the day’s work began early. Her care for her household begins before the day does. The poem presents this as a picture of diligence, not a rule that every woman must rise before dawn.

“And provides food for her household,”

Her first concern is that those under her roof are fed. She makes sure the household has what it needs for the day.

“And a portion for her maidservants.”

Her care reaches those who serve her. The maidservants receive their portion, either their food or their assigned tasks for the day. No one in her house is overlooked, including those of lower station.

As a layered reading, her rising while it is still night pictures the Bride’s watchfulness through the darkness of this age, ready for the Bridegroom, as in the parable where “at midnight a cry was heard: ‘Behold, the bridegroom is coming’” (Matthew 25:6). The picture is illustrative and does not set out an end-time timetable.
15.notes: The NLT interprets the last line as planning the day’s work for her servant girls, taking “portion” as assigned tasks; the ESV and NASB read “portions” for her maidens.

16.brief: Considering a field carefully, she buys it, then plants a vineyard from what she has earned. Her wisdom extends to business, as she weighs a decision carefully and invests her profits in something that will keep producing.
16.explain:
“She considers a field and buys it;”

Her wisdom reaches into business. She does not buy on impulse. She considers the field, weighing its value and its usefulness, and then acts decisively. Careful thought followed by action is a mark of wisdom throughout Proverbs. The verse shows a woman trusted to make significant decisions about property and the household’s future.

“From her profits she plants a vineyard.”

She invests what she has earned in something that will keep producing. A vineyard takes years before it bears fully, so planting one is an act of foresight and patience. Her profits do not go to waste or to show; they go into the household’s long-term good.
16.notes: The Hebrew reads from the fruit of her palms, which the ESV and KJV render “the fruit of her hands,” tying her purchase to her own labor. For “buys,” the KJV margin notes that the Hebrew verb is literally taketh.

17.brief: Girding herself with strength, she makes her arms strong. The picture of a woman tying up her garments for hard work shows her meeting her tasks with vigor and readiness.
17.explain:
“She girds herself with strength,”

To gird oneself was to tie up long garments with a belt so they would not hinder vigorous work or movement. She prepares for her tasks the way a worker or a soldier prepares for his. The word “strength” fits the poem’s description of her as a woman of valor. Her strength is physical and practical, and it is also the readiness of a person who meets her duties without hesitation.

“And strengthens her arms.”

Her arms are strong for the work before her. The repetition of strength in both lines emphasizes the point: this woman is no fragile ornament. She works hard, and her strength grows as she uses it. The poem honors physical labor done well and willingly as part of a wise and godly life.
17.notes: The Hebrew says that she girds her loins with strength, the wording the KJV keeps. The ESV reads “dresses herself” with strength.

18.brief: She sees that her trading is profitable, and her lamp does not go out at night, a poetic picture of diligence and watchful care rather than a demand for sleepless labor or a checklist laid on every woman. Read at the layered level, her burning lamp pictures the Bride’s watchful faith through the darkness of this age, ready for the Bridegroom (Matthew 25:1–13).
18.explain:
“She perceives that her merchandise is good,”

She knows her trading is profitable. She has tested her goods and her dealings and found them good. Her confidence rests on careful work and honest trade, and she can see the fruit of her labor.

“And her lamp does not go out by night.”

Her lamp still burning at night pictures a household that is supplied and cared for, where the oil has not run out and her care continues after dark. Proverbs uses the opposite picture for the wicked, whose lamp will be put out: “The lamp of the wicked will be put out” (24:20). The line is a poetic picture of diligence and watchful care, not a demand for sleepless labor or a checklist laid on every woman.

Read at the layered level, her burning lamp pictures the Bride’s watchful faith through the darkness of this age, ready for the Bridegroom, like the wise virgins whose lamps were trimmed when he came (Matthew 25:1–13).
18.notes:
In Hebrew “She perceives” is literally she tastes, as the KJV margin notes: she has tasted her trading and found it good.

The NLT reads “her lamp burns late into the night,” and the ESV and NASB read “at night.”

19.brief: Her hands reach for the distaff and hold the spindle, spinning the thread herself. The same hands that do business also do the patient, ordinary work of the home.
19.explain:
“She stretches out her hands to the distaff,”

The distaff held the raw wool or flax, and the spindle twisted it into thread. Spinning was steady, patient, ordinary work done by hand. She reaches out to it herself, even though she manages servants, trade, and property.

“And her hand holds the spindle.”

The same hands that conduct business also do the quiet, repetitive work of the home. Nothing is beneath her. The poem honors the humble task as much as the large decision, and both are part of the wisdom it praises. The next verse will show those same hands reaching out to the poor.
19.notes:
In Hebrew the words for the hands form a crossing pattern across 31:19–20: hands and then palms in 31:19, palm and then hands in 31:20. The same Hebrew verb, translated “stretches out” in 31:19 and “reaches out” in 31:20, appears in both verses. The hands that reach to the spindle are the hands that reach to the needy.

The KJV reverses the two tools, placing her hands on the spindle and the distaff in her hands.

20.brief: Those same hands open to the poor and reach out to the needy. Her diligence is matched by generosity, so that her household’s abundance overflows to others.
20.explain:
“She extends her hand to the poor,”

Her diligence is matched by generosity. The hand that works hard does not close around what it has gained. She extends it to the poor, giving freely from the abundance her work has produced. Proverbs teaches that “He who has pity on the poor lends to the LORD” (19:17), and here that pity is a settled habit of her life.

“Yes, she reaches out her hands to the needy.”

The second line repeats and intensifies the first. “Yes” adds emphasis, and “hands” is now plural: she reaches out fully. Her household’s abundance overflows to people outside it. A wise woman’s success is not measured only by what she stores up but by what she gives away. In her, the book’s many sayings about generosity to the poor become a living portrait.
20.notes: The Hebrew verb behind “extends” means to spread out, as the KJV margin’s “She spreadeth” shows, picturing an open hand. The ESV reads “opens” for “extends.”

21.brief: She is not afraid of snow for her household, because all of them are clothed in scarlet. Her foresight has dressed them warmly in rich cloth before winter comes; at a deeper level, the scarlet pictures her household covered by the blood of Christ.
21.explain:
“She is not afraid of snow for her household,”

Snow brings the cold of winter, and a household must be ready for it. She faces it without fear. Her calm does not come from wishful thinking but from preparation already made.

“For all her household is clothed with scarlet.”

Long before winter comes, she has dressed her whole household in scarlet. The verse names only the color, but scarlet cloth was a mark of quality and honor (2 Samuel 1:24), and the point of the line is that everyone in her house is well and warmly clothed; the cloth was probably wool, though the verse does not say so. She has provided the best for everyone in her house, not only for herself. Her foresight removes the reason for fear.

At a deeper, layered level, the scarlet pictures her household covered by the blood of Christ. As a household clothed in scarlet need not fear the cold, those covered by His blood need not fear what is coming. This reading is a spiritual layer added to the plain picture of warm clothing, which remains the verse’s natural sense.
21.notes: The KJV margin offers “double garments” as an alternative to “scarlet.” The NLT interprets the line simply as “warm clothes.”

22.brief: She makes fine coverings for herself and dresses in fine linen and purple, the cloth of honor. Her dignity shows in what she wears, and in the layered reading her fine linen recalls the Bride arrayed in fine linen, clean and bright, at the marriage of the Lamb (Revelation 19:7–8).
22.explain:
“She makes tapestry for herself;”

Having cared for her household, she also provides for herself. The “tapestry” is woven coverings, likely for her bed, made by her own skill. The poem does not count it a fault that she enjoys well-made things.

“Her clothing is fine linen and purple.”

Fine linen and purple were the cloth of honor, worn by the wealthy and by royalty. Purple dye was especially costly. Her dignity shows in what she wears, and the clothing matches the worth of the woman. This is not vanity; her appearance reflects a life of honorable work and good order.

In the layered reading, her fine linen recalls the Bride at the marriage of the Lamb, to whom “it was granted to be arrayed in fine linen, clean and bright, for the fine linen is the righteous acts of the saints” (Revelation 19:8).
22.notes: The ESV and NASB read “coverings” for “tapestry,” and the ESV connects them with her bed. The KJV reads “silk” for “fine linen.”

23.brief: Her husband is known and respected in the city gates, where he sits among the elders of the land. Her faithful management at home supports his standing in public, and the layered reading sees Christ, the Bridegroom, seated in honor at the Father’s right hand.
23.explain:
“Her husband is known in the gates,”

The city gate was where the elders met, legal cases were heard, and the business of the town was conducted. Her husband is known and respected there. Part of the reason is the household she manages. Her faithfulness at home frees him to serve in public, and her good reputation adds to his. A man whose household is in order can be trusted with the affairs of the community.

“When he sits among the elders of the land.”

He takes his seat among the elders, the leaders who governed and judged. The verse shows how a household’s life and a community’s life are joined. The wisdom practiced at home reaches the gate.

In the layered reading of the poem, the husband known in the gates pictures Christ, the Bridegroom, seated in honor at the Father’s right hand, for He “sat down at the right hand of the Majesty on high” (Hebrews 1:3).
23.notes: The NLT reads “city gates,” and it says her husband is “well known” there.

24.brief: Linen garments come from her hands for sale, and she supplies sashes to the merchants. Her home is also a place of skilled, profitable work that reaches into the marketplace.
24.explain:
“She makes linen garments and sells them,”

Her home is also a place of production. She makes linen garments and sells them. Her skill reaches the market and brings in income. The poem presents a woman whose work at home is serious, skilled, and profitable.

“And supplies sashes for the merchants.”

She also supplies sashes, or belts, to the traders. Merchants depend on her goods. The verse closes the circle begun in 31:13: the wool and flax she sought out have become goods that leave her house and earn their place in the wider economy. Her industry is not limited to her own household; it serves the community as well.
24.notes: The Hebrew word translated “merchants” is the name Canaanite, the people who lived in the land before Israel. Here the name is used for a trader. The NASB reads “belts” for “sashes,” and the KJV “girdles.”

25.brief: Strength and honor are her clothing, and she can rejoice at the time to come. Her truest garments are her character, and because she has prepared well and lives in the fear of the LORD, she faces the future without fear.
25.explain:
“Strength and honor are her clothing;”

The poem moves from her garments to her character. Her truest clothing is strength and honor. These are what people see when they look at her, more than linen or purple. She wears her character as visibly as a garment, and it suits her well.

“She shall rejoice in time to come.”

Because she has prepared well and lives in the fear of the LORD, she faces the future without fear. Whatever the days ahead may bring, she meets them with confidence and joy, not anxiety. Her preparation for winter (31:21) is one example of a whole life lived with an eye to what is coming.

As a layered reading, she pictures the Bride clothed in strength and unafraid of the future, rejoicing in what is to come because her Bridegroom holds it.
25.notes: The ESV, NASB, and NLT read “dignity” for “honor.” The ESV and NLT read “laughs” for “rejoice,” and the NASB says she “smiles” at the future.

26.brief: Wisdom comes out when she opens her mouth, and the law of kindness governs her tongue. Her words carry both insight and steady kindness, the speech of a woman taught by the fear of the LORD.
26.explain:
“She opens her mouth with wisdom,”

After her hands, the poem turns to her words. When she speaks, wisdom comes out. Her speech is thoughtful, insightful, and helpful. She does not speak rashly or foolishly, and others can learn from what she says. In a book so concerned with the tongue, this is high praise.

“And on her tongue is the law of kindness.”

Kindness governs her tongue. “Law” here means teaching or instruction, so her words carry kind instruction, guidance given with steady love. Her speech is both wise and gentle, truthful and generous. The Hebrew word for kindness is the word often used for God’s steadfast love and faithfulness. Her speech reflects the character of the God she fears.
26.notes:
The Hebrew word translated “law” means instruction or teaching. It is the same word used for “the law of your mother” in 1:8, so this woman gives the kind of instruction the book’s opening urged a son to keep. The ESV and NASB read “teaching” for “law.”

The Hebrew phrase behind “the law of kindness” literally means instruction of kindness: teaching given in kindness.

27.brief: Watching over the ways of her household, she never eats the bread of idleness. Unlike the lazy man of the book’s earlier portraits, she gives careful attention to everything entrusted to her.
27.explain:
“She watches over the ways of her household,”

She is attentive. Like a watchman on a wall, she keeps watch over what is happening in her home, the conduct of its members, its needs, and its affairs. Her oversight is not suspicion but care.

“And does not eat the bread of idleness.”

She is not idle, and the bread of idleness has no place in her life. The contrast with the lazy man of the book’s earlier portraits is clear, the one who folds his hands to sleep while poverty comes on him (6:9–11). She gives careful attention to what is entrusted to her. Her diligence is not anxious busyness but faithful stewardship of her home.
27.notes:
In Hebrew “watches over” is a verb form that describes ongoing action: she is one who keeps watch over her household. The ESV and NASB read “looks well” for “watches over.”

Proverbs 31:28–31 — A Woman Who Fears the LORD Shall Be Praised

28.brief: Her children rise up and call her blessed, and her husband adds his praise. Those who know her best, at home, are the first to honor her.
28.explain:
“Her children rise up and call her blessed;”

The poem now turns to praise, and it begins at home. Her children rise up, a gesture of respect, and call her blessed, acknowledging the good of her life. Those who know her best, who have seen her daily life up close, are the first to honor her. Praise from people who live with someone carries special weight.

“Her husband also, and he praises her:”

Her husband joins the children in praising her. The man whose heart trusts her (31:11) now speaks his praise aloud, and the colon introduces his own words in the next verse. A husband who praises his wife publicly honors both her and the God who gave her to him.
28.notes: The NASB and NLT read “bless her” for “call her blessed.”

29.brief: Her husband’s praise is given in his own words: “Many daughters have done well, But you excel them all.” He has found the woman of worth that verse 10 asked about, and he says so.
29.explain:
“‘Many daughters have done well,”

These are her husband’s own words. He acknowledges that many women have done well. The Hebrew word behind “done well” is the same word that described her as “virtuous” in 31:10, so the line means many women have shown strength, worth, and excellence. His praise of her does not belittle other women; it honors them.

“But you excel them all.’”

Yet in his eyes she surpasses them all. This is the language of a husband who has found the woman of worth that 31:10 asked about, and he says so directly to her. The praise is personal and wholehearted. It is not a ranking of women for others to measure themselves against, but a husband’s grateful delight in the wife God has given him.
29.notes: The KJV’s “done virtuously” keeps the link with “virtuous” in 31:10, and the NASB reads “nobly.” The KJV margin offers “gotten riches,” because the same Hebrew noun can also mean wealth.

30.brief: Charm can deceive and beauty fades, but a woman who fears the LORD will be praised. Here lies the source of all her worth, so the same honor belongs to every woman who fears Him, whether single, widowed, or married, and the book ends where it began, with the fear of the LORD, a right view of God, as the beginning of knowledge (1:7).
30.explain:
“Charm is deceitful and beauty is passing,”

Charm can deceive, for a pleasing manner may hide an empty or false heart. Beauty is passing, like a breath that quickly vanishes. Neither is condemned, but neither can bear the weight of a life’s worth. The poem has said almost nothing about her appearance; it has described her character and her works.

“But a woman who fears the LORD, she shall be praised.”

Here lies the source of everything the poem has praised. She fears the LORD. Her strength, diligence, generosity, wisdom, and kindness all grow from a right view of God. The book began with “The fear of the LORD is the beginning of knowledge” (1:7), and it ends with a woman who lives that truth. Because her praise rests on the fear of the LORD and not on achievement, marital status, or a list of tasks, the same honor belongs to every woman who fears Him, whether single, widowed, or married. The poem is a portrait to admire, not a standard to burden anyone.
30.notes: The Hebrew word translated “passing” means a breath or vapor, something that quickly disappears. The ESV, NASB, and KJV read “vain,” and the KJV reads “Favour” for “Charm.”

31.brief: Give her the reward her hands have earned, and let her own works praise her in the gates. The book closes with public honor for a woman whose life of wisdom speaks for itself in the city gates, an echo of the public places where Wisdom first cried out (1:21).
31.explain:
“Give her of the fruit of her hands,”

The poem ends with a call to give her what she has earned. Her work deserves its reward. “The fruit of her hands” is the result of all the labor described in the poem, and she should share in it. This is justice as well as praise.

“And let her own works praise her in the gates.”

The final line takes her praise into public. The gates were where the elders sat (31:23) and where reputations were made and judged. Her works speak for themselves there, needing no further words. The book that began with Wisdom crying out “At the openings of the gates in the city” (1:21) ends with a wise woman praised in those same gates. Wisdom called in public at the start; here wisdom lived out receives public honor at the close. Proverbs ends not with a rule but with a life, built on the fear of the LORD, whose works bear witness to the wisdom behind them.
31.notes: The NLT reads “Reward her for all she has done,” and it interprets the second line as her deeds publicly declaring her praise.
